- **Mobile Fit**: Dockview explicitly says it is touch and mobile ready, and its drag-and-drop documentation describes pointer events plus long-press-to-drag so taps and native scrolling continue to work -> prefer it over desktop-only docking libraries when phone use matters. [executive_summary[0]] [8] [executive_summary[1]] [34]
- **License Fit**: The project repository identifies the library as open source and the repository includes an MIT license -> it satisfies the stated licensing constraint, subject to retaining the license notice. [executive_summary[2]] [6] [executive_summary[3]] [9]
- **Correct Boundary**: super.engineering is a native macOS agent workspace with durable workspaces, Git worktrees, terminals, chat, and diff review, not a UI library -> Dockview supplies the pane mechanics, while your application must supply those workspace semantics. [executive_summary[4]] [23]
- **Runner-Up**: FlexLayout is also MIT and React-focused, with resizable and movable tabsets, edge docking, floating panels, persistence, accessibility, and mobile support described in its repository -> choose it if a React-only, model-driven layout API is more important than Dockview's explicit mobile positioning. [executive_summary[5]] [11]
- **Avoid a License Trap**: React-Dockable is a plausible visual fit, but its repository lists separate commercial and noncommercial license files and states that commercial use requires a commercial license or sponsorship -> do not treat it as an MIT substitute. [executive_summary[6]] [26]
content.why_dockview_fits_the_super_engineering_:
The useful part of the super.engineering reference is not its macOS implementation; it is the relationship between durable workspaces and rearrangeable tools. Its documentation describes projects grouped into durable workspaces, task isolation through Git-backed worktrees, terminals and chat tied to the code they change, and a surface for reviewing diffs before merging. The product page also presents tabs and workspaces as a way to run several coding agents in one place. [why_dockview_fits_the_super_engineering_pattern[0]] [23] [why_dockview_fits_the_super_engineering_pattern[1]] [21]

Dockview maps well to the presentation layer of that model. Its documented primitives - tabs, groups, grids, split views, drag and drop, floating panels, and popouts - are enough to represent an agent session, terminal, diff, file browser, browser preview, and logs as movable surfaces. The mechanism is separation of concerns: Dockview manages geometry and panel interaction; your state model manages workspace identity, project membership, active agent, permissions, persistence, and routing. [why_dockview_fits_the_super_engineering_pattern[2]] [6] [why_dockview_fits_the_super_engineering_pattern[3]] [8]

The important implication is that Dockview is an alternative to Paseo's nested-workspace UI, not a replacement for Paseo's orchestration product. That is an advantage if the goal is to build a custom experience: keep the agent and repository model independent from the layout tree, then serialize both separately. A mobile client can show the same workspace state as a single active pane with a drawer or bottom sheet, while desktop can expose splits and floating panels. This responsive policy is an implementation recommendation, not a claim that Dockview automatically creates the complete Paseo product.
content.candidate_comparison:
| Candidate | License and scope | Docking capability | Mobile evidence | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Dockview** | Open source; MIT repository license; React, Vue, Angular, and vanilla TypeScript support | Tabs, groups, grids, split views, drag and drop, floating panels, popouts | Official site says touch and mobile ready; docs describe long-press-to-drag and native-scroll behavior | **Recommended** |
| **FlexLayout** | MIT; React layout manager | Multiple tabsets, resizing, moving, edge docking, floating panels, popouts, serialized models | Mobile support is listed in the project README | Strong React-only alternative |
| **Golden Layout** | MIT JavaScript layout manager | Components arranged and rearranged with drag and drop | The reviewed official sources establish docking, but do not make as direct a mobile-readiness claim | Desktop-oriented fallback |

The table points to a specific trade-off. FlexLayout is the strongest alternative when its React model and serialized layout state align with the application, while Golden Layout is a legitimate MIT docking option but has weaker evidence for the mobile requirement in the sources reviewed. Dockview wins because mobile is not merely inferred from responsive CSS; it is an explicit product claim backed by a documented touch gesture design. content.reference_case_super_engineering_as_the_:
super.engineering makes a clear product decision: it treats coding-agent work as durable context rather than a collection of disposable windows. The documented workspace contains projects, isolated Git-backed tasks, terminal and chat sessions, and diff review. Its documented outcome is that a user can return to the same workspace and continue work with the relevant sessions and code context intact. [reference_case_super_engineering_as_the_design_target[0]] [23]

That case reveals what a UI library can and cannot do. Dockview can implement the visible interaction decision - dock, split, reorder, detach, and restore panels - but it does not create the durable context, worktree isolation, agent lifecycle, or merge workflow described by super.engineering. The recommended architecture is therefore to make `workspaceId`, project/task identity, session identity, and layout state separate persisted records. The layout record can change when a user rearranges panes without corrupting the agent or repository record.

For mobile, the same case argues against shrinking a desktop layout until every pane is unreadable. Use Dockview for the shared panel model, but switch the presentation policy at a narrow breakpoint: one active surface, an explicit pane switcher, and a quick return path to the workspace overview. Long-press drag support and native scrolling address touch interaction; the single-surface policy addresses information density. This is the practical way to achieve a good mobile experience rather than assuming that desktop docking automatically becomes mobile-friendly. [reference_case_super_engineering_as_the_design_target[1]] [8] [reference_case_super_engineering_as_the_design_target[2]] [34]
content.synthesis_and_recommendation:
Across mechanism, scope, and trade-offs, Dockview is the best fit for the stated constraint set. Dockview has the clearest mobile evidence and broad framework support, but it is a layout engine, so the application must build nested workspace semantics around it. FlexLayout offers a more explicitly React and model-oriented alternative with a broad docking feature set and stated mobile support, but Dockview's touch documentation makes the mobile requirement easier to defend. Golden Layout is mature as a general JavaScript docking manager and is MIT licensed, but the reviewed evidence does not establish the same mobile emphasis. [synthesis_and_recommendation[0]] [6] [synthesis_and_recommendation[1]] [11] [synthesis_and_recommendation[2]] [16]

The non-obvious tension is between reproducing a rich desktop workspace and preserving mobile usability. More docking freedom is valuable on a large screen but can produce a cramped, gesture-conflicting phone UI. The decision should therefore be **Dockview plus a responsive workspace policy**, not Dockview alone: use docked multi-pane layouts on desktop, a focused-pane navigation model on mobile, and keep workspace/session persistence in application state. If the project is strictly React and its model serialization is the decisive factor, evaluate FlexLayout in a short prototype; otherwise, start with Dockview.
